notes.front: What is infrastructure as code (IaC)?
notes.back: Defining and deploying infrastructure and its configuration through code files, instead of by hand in a portal or console.
notes.explanation: The Well-Architected guidance makes it the standard for infrastructure deployments so they follow the same practices as software development.
notes.example: Like a recipe card for a kitchen: anyone following it gets the same dish, unlike a cook who improvises each time.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Ansible?
notes.back: An open-source product that automates cloud provisioning, configuration management and application deployments.
notes.explanation: With it you can provision virtual machines, containers, networks and complete cloud infrastructures in Azure.
notes.example: Like a site foreman with a written plan who both builds the rooms and fits them out, room after room.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Using Ansible with Azure”, “Using Ansible with Azure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-dev-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Ansible is an open-source product that automates cloud provisioning, configuration management, and application deployments. Using Ansible you can provision virtual machines, containers, and network and complete cloud infrastructures.

notes.front: What is an Ansible playbook?
notes.back: A file, written in YAML, that directs Ansible to configure your environment.
notes.explanation: Playbooks are coded in YAML so that people can read them.
notes.example: Like a checklist a pilot reads before take-off, but one that Ansible carries out on each server itself.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Using Ansible with Azure”, “Ansible playbooks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-dev-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Ansible playbooks allow you to direct Ansible to configure your environment. Playbooks are coded using YAML so as to be human-readable.

notes.front: What is Ansible dynamic inventory?
notes.back: An Ansible feature that pulls its inventory of hosts from Azure resources, so you can manage tagged deployments.
notes.explanation: You tag existing Azure deployments and then manage those tagged deployments through Ansible.
notes.example: Like a delivery driver whose route is rebuilt each morning from the day's orders instead of a printed list from last month.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Using Ansible with Azure”, “Manage deployments with dynamic inventory” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-dev-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Using the Ansible dynamic inventory feature, you can pull inventory from Azure resources. You can then tag your existing Azure deployments and manage those tagged deployments through Ansible.

notes.front: What is a Chef service connection in Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: A stored, secured connection from Azure Pipelines to a Chef automation server.
notes.explanation: Its required parameters include the server address, a node name and the client key from the Chef `.pem` file.
notes.example: Like a saved login for a supplier's portal that every pipeline in the project can be allowed to use.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Service connections”, “Chef service connection” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use the following parameters to define and secure a connection to a Chef automation server.

notes.front: What is PowerShell desired state configuration (DSC)?
notes.back: A PowerShell approach in which machines are assigned declarative configurations and brought to, and reported against, that desired state.
notes.explanation: Azure Automation State Configuration lets you write, compile and assign DSC configurations for nodes in any cloud or on premises.
notes.example: Like a hotel room standard: the housekeeper is told how the room must look, not each move to make, and reports rooms that do not match.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview”, “Why use Azure Automation State Configuration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can easily enable machines, assign them declarative configurations, and view reports showing each machine's compliance with the desired state you specify.

notes.front: What is Azure Automation State Configuration?
notes.back: An Azure configuration management service for writing, managing and compiling PowerShell DSC configurations and assigning them to nodes.
notes.explanation: It imports DSC resources and assigns configurations in the cloud, but it retires on 30 September 2027, with Azure Machine Configuration named as its successor.
notes.example: Like a central office that issues the room standard to every hotel in a chain and collects their inspection reports.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview”, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Automation State Configuration is an Azure configuration management service that allows you to write, manage, and compile PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) configurations for nodes in any cloud or on-premises datacenter.

notes.front: What is the built-in pull server in Azure Automation State Configuration?
notes.back: A DSC pull server from which target nodes automatically receive configurations and to which they report compliance.
notes.explanation: Because Azure Automation provides it, you do not need to set up and maintain your own pull server.
notes.example: Like a news feed each branch office checks for updated rules, instead of head office phoning every branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview”, “Built-in pull server” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Target nodes can automatically receive configurations, conform to the desired state, and report on their compliance. The built-in pull server in Azure Automation eliminates the need to set up and maintain your own pull server.

notes.front: What is Azure Machine Configuration?
notes.back: An Azure Policy feature that audits or configures operating system settings as code on Azure and Arc-enabled hybrid machines.
notes.explanation: You can use it per machine or orchestrate it at scale with Azure Policy.
notes.example: Like a building inspector who can either just write up a flat that breaks the rules, or also fix it on the spot.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Policy's machine configuration feature provides native capability to audit or configure operating system settings as code for machines running in Azure and hybrid [Arc-enabled machines][01].

notes.front: What is Azure Deployment Environments?
notes.back: A service that lets development teams spin up app infrastructure on demand from project-based templates.
notes.explanation: Its templates set consistency and best practice while maximising security; note that the service retires on 22 February 2027.
notes.example: Like a tool library where staff borrow a ready-assembled kit instead of buying and assembling their own.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?”, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Deployment Environments empowers development teams to quickly and easily spin up app infrastructure with project-based templates that establish consistency and best practices while maximizing security.

notes.front: What is a dev center in Azure Deployment Environments?
notes.back: A collection of projects that need similar settings.
notes.explanation: Platform engineers use it to manage catalogs of templates and the environment types teams can create.
notes.example: Like a regional office that sets shared rules for all the teams under it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Dev centers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A dev center is a collection of projects that require similar settings.

notes.front: What is a project in Azure Deployment Environments?
notes.back: A team or business function in the organisation; it inherits all the settings of the one dev center it is associated with.
notes.explanation: Each project can belong to only one dev center.
notes.example: Like one department inside the regional office, following the office's rules.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Projects” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In Deployment Environments, a project represents a team or business function within the organization. When you associate a project with a dev center, all the settings for the dev center are automatically applied to the project.

notes.front: What is an environment type in Azure Deployment Environments?
notes.back: A kind of environment teams may create, such as dev, test, sandbox, preproduction or production, with its own settings.
notes.explanation: You can name the types to match your organisation's own terms.
notes.example: Like ticket classes on a train: each class has its own rules and price, and you choose the names.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Dev center environment types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can define the types of environments that development teams can create: for example, dev, test, sandbox, preproduction, or production.

notes.front: What is a catalog in Azure Deployment Environments?
notes.back: A curated set of IaC templates that development teams can use to create environments.
notes.explanation: It is attached to a dev center or to a project.
notes.example: Like a restaurant menu: diners pick from dishes the chef has approved.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Catalogs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Catalogs help you provide a set of curated IaC templates that your development teams can use to create environments.

notes.front: What is an environment definition in Azure Deployment Environments?
notes.back: An IaC template plus an environment file that acts as its manifest.
notes.explanation: The template defines the environment and the environment file gives metadata about the template.
notes.example: Like a flat-pack wardrobe: the parts and instructions, plus a label on the box saying what it is.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Environment definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An environment definition is a combination of an IaC template and an environment file that acts as a manifest.

notes.front: How should infrastructure changes, including configuration changes, be deployed according to the Well-Architected guidance?
notes.back: Only through code, deployed by continuous integration and delivery pipelines.
notes.explanation: The policy keeps deployments consistent and reduces configuration drift between environments.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which kind of IaC tool does the Well-Architected guidance prefer, and why?
notes.back: Declarative tools: their files only describe the desired end state, so they are simpler than step-by-step imperative files.
notes.explanation: Declarative files also avoid the technical debt of maintaining imperative deployment scripts.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Prefer declarative over imperative tools”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What should IaC templates use so one standard set of resources can deploy any environment in the promotion path?
notes.back: Parameters, variables and configuration files.
notes.explanation: Values such as size, count, name, location and configuration settings are the ones to abstract.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Support multiple environments”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Should production and test use different IaC files?
notes.back: No. Use the same IaC assets, one file adapted to each environment, as far as possible.
notes.explanation: The guidance gives separate Terraform files for production and test as the thing to avoid.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Support multiple environments”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For desired state configuration, which tool does the guidance give as an example for virtual machines, and which for Kubernetes clusters?
notes.back: Ansible for virtual machines; Flux for Kubernetes clusters.
notes.explanation: A deployment tool such as Bicep might not be the best tool for every management operation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Use the right tool for the task”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which standards should IaC share with application code, according to the Well-Architected guidance?
notes.back: Version control, branching, code promotion and quality standards, all identical.
notes.explanation: The guidance also suggests keeping IaC assets alongside the application code.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Treat IaC and application code the same”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which set of Ansible modules lets you create and orchestrate infrastructure on Azure?
notes.back: The Ansible cloud modules for Azure.
notes.explanation: Modules run directly on remote hosts or through playbooks, and users can write their own.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Using Ansible with Azure”, “Ansible modules” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-dev-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For interacting with Azure services, Ansible includes a suite of Ansible cloud modules. These modules enable you to create and orchestrate your infrastructure on Azure.

notes.front: If you are not ready to manage machine configuration from the cloud, how can you still use Azure Automation State Configuration?
notes.back: As a report-only endpoint: push configurations through DSC and view reporting in Azure Automation.
notes.explanation: In that mode you push configurations to machines instead of having them pull.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview”, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you aren't ready to manage machine configuration from the cloud, you can use Azure Automation State Configuration as a report-only endpoint. This feature allows you to set (push) configurations through DSC and view reporting details in Azure Automation.

notes.front: What advantage over using DSC outside Azure does Azure Automation State Configuration give at scale?
notes.back: Quick, easy scalability across thousands of machines from a central, secure location.
notes.explanation: You enable machines, assign configurations and view compliance reports in one place.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview”, “Why use Azure Automation State Configuration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This service enables scalability across thousands of machines quickly and easily from a central, secure location.

notes.front: Which machines can Azure Automation target with its pull server?
notes.back: Virtual or physical Windows machines, in the cloud or on premises; the page still lists Linux, but Linux support has retired.
notes.explanation: Automation DSC for Linux retired on 30 September 2023, so only Windows targets remain supported.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview”, “Built-in pull server” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Automation can target virtual or physical Windows or Linux machines, in the cloud or on-premises.

notes.front: On what date did Azure Automation DSC for Linux retire?
notes.back: 30 September 2023.
notes.explanation: The announcement it links to is about moving to Azure Policy's guest configuration feature, the older name for Machine Configuration.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automation DSC for Linux retirement announcement” (include file) (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Automation DSC for Linux has retired on 30 September 2023.

notes.front: Are machine configurations the same thing as policy definitions?
notes.back: No. They are distinct; Machine Configuration uses Azure Policy to assign configurations to machines dynamically.
notes.explanation: You can also assign configurations to machines manually.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Configurations are distinct from policy definitions. Machine configuration uses Azure Policy to dynamically assign configurations to machines.

notes.front: Which Machine Configuration enforcement mode only reports on the state of the machine?
notes.back: Audit.
notes.explanation: It changes nothing on the machine.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “Enforcement Modes for Custom Policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Audit                 | Only report on the state of the machine

notes.front: Which Machine Configuration enforcement mode applies the configuration and then monitors for changes, without correcting them?
notes.back: Apply and Monitor.
notes.explanation: It sits between reporting only and correcting drift.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “Enforcement Modes for Custom Policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Apply and Monitor     | Configuration applied to the machine and then monitored for changes

notes.front: Which Machine Configuration enforcement mode brings a machine back into conformance if drift occurs?
notes.back: Apply and Autocorrect.
notes.explanation: Of the three enforcement modes, only this one corrects drift.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “Enforcement Modes for Custom Policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Apply and Autocorrect | Configuration applied to the machine and brought back into conformance if drift occurs

notes.front: Which scale set orchestration mode does Machine Configuration support, and which does it not?
notes.back: It supports Flex, but not Uniform.
notes.explanation: Custom machine images are supported as long as they run a listed operating system.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “Supported client types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Machine Configuration doesn't support VMSS uniform but does support [VMSS Flex][46].

notes.front: What does Resource Manager convert a template into when you deploy it?
notes.back: Operations on the Resource Manager programming interface, sent to each resource provider.
notes.explanation: The `apiVersion` set for each resource in the template is the version used for that operation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Templates overview”, “Template deployment process” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you deploy a template, Resource Manager converts the template into REST API operations.

notes.front: How does Resource Manager handle interdependent resources in a template deployment?
notes.back: It creates them in the correct order and deploys in parallel where it can.
notes.explanation: Parallel deployment makes the deployment finish faster than a serial one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Templates overview”, “Why choose ARM templates?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Resource Manager orchestrates the deployment of interdependent resources so they're created in the correct order. When possible, Resource Manager deploys resources in parallel, so your deployments finish faster than serial deployments.

notes.front: What does Resource Manager check before starting a template deployment?
notes.back: It validates the template, deploying only after it passes.
notes.explanation: This makes the deployment less likely to stop half-finished.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Templates overview”, “Why choose ARM templates?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Your template is deployed only after passing validation. Resource Manager checks the template before starting the deployment to make sure it succeeds. Your deployment is less likely to stop in a half-finished state.

notes.front: Which Azure Pipelines task lets you continuously build and deploy ARM template projects?
notes.back: The Resource Manager template task.
notes.explanation: Integrating templates with release pipelines automates infrastructure updates alongside the application.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Templates overview”, “Why choose ARM templates?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This integration automates your release pipelines for fast and reliable application and infrastructure updates. By using Azure DevOps and Resource Manager template task, you can use Azure Pipelines to continuously build and deploy ARM template projects.

notes.front: When can you use a new Azure resource type, or a new version of one, in a Bicep file?
notes.back: As soon as the resource provider introduces it, including preview versions.
notes.explanation: You do not wait for tools to be updated before using new services.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Bicep?”, “Benefits of Bicep” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: As soon as a resource provider introduces new resource types and API versions, you can use them in your Bicep file.

notes.front: Where is the state of a Bicep deployment kept?
notes.back: Azure stores all state; there are no state files to manage.
notes.explanation: So teams can collaborate without sharing a state file.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Bicep?”, “Benefits of Bicep” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **No state or state files to manage**: Azure stores all states. You can collaborate with others and be confident that your updates are handled as expected.

notes.front: How does Bicep syntax compare with the equivalent JSON template?
notes.back: More concise and easier to read, and declarative.
notes.explanation: Bicep does not require prior knowledge of programming languages.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Bicep?”, “Benefits of Bicep” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When compared to the equivalent JSON template, Bicep files are more concise and easier to read. Bicep doesn't require prior knowledge of programming languages.

notes.front: Does the what-if operation change any existing resources?
notes.back: No. It only predicts the changes a deployment would make.
notes.explanation: You can run it from Azure PowerShell or the Azure CLI, among other options.
notes.source: Microsoft, “ARM template deployment what-if operation”, “ARM template deployment what-if operation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The what-if operation doesn't make any changes to existing resources. Instead, it predicts the changes if the specified template is deployed.

notes.front: Which Azure CLI switch on `az deployment group create` previews changes and asks before deploying?
notes.back: `--confirm-with-what-if` (short form `-c`).
notes.explanation: In Azure PowerShell, `-Confirm` on `New-AzResourceGroupDeployment` does the same.
notes.source: Microsoft, “ARM template deployment what-if operation”, “Azure CLI” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use the `--confirm-with-what-if` switch (or its short form `-c`) to preview the changes and get prompted to continue with the deployment.

notes.front: By what date must Azure Deployment Environments workflows move to another service?
notes.back: 22 February 2027, when Azure Deployment Environments retires.
notes.explanation: The note asks users to move to a Microsoft service, an Azure service or a partner solution.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Deployment Environments retirement note” (include file) (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Transition your Azure Deployment Environments workflows to a Microsoft service, Azure service, or partner solution by 22 February 2027. Azure Deployment Environments retires on this date.

notes.front: On what basis can platform engineers apply Azure governance in Deployment Environments?
notes.back: The type of environment, such as sandbox, testing, staging or production.
notes.explanation: They also control what resource configuration developers can create and track environments across projects.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?”, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: They can apply Azure governance based on the type of environment, such as sandbox, testing, staging, or production.

notes.front: Which Deployment Environments scenario lets development teams connect lifecycle environments, from development to production, to their pipelines?
notes.back: Environments as part of a continuous integration and delivery pipeline.
notes.explanation: Central teams can then track costs and security alerts across projects and dev centers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?”, “Environments as part of a CI/CD pipeline” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By using Deployment Environments, developers can incorporate different types of product lifecycle environments (such as development, testing, staging, preproduction, and production) into a CI/CD pipeline.

notes.front: Which Deployment Environments scenario creates ad hoc environments that mimic formal test environments, before code is checked in?
notes.back: On-demand test environments.
notes.explanation: Reusable templates make these ad hoc environments quick to create.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?”, “On-demand test environments” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Developers can create ad hoc environments that mimic their formal development or test environments to test a new capability before checking in the code and running a pipeline.

notes.front: In which Deployment Environments scenario does a project act as a container for transient activities, deleted with all its resources afterwards?
notes.back: Training, hands-on labs and hackathons.
notes.explanation: Each user can create identical, isolated environments.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?”, “Training, hands-on labs, and hackathons” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A project in Deployment Environments acts as a container for transient activities like workshops, hands-on labs, training, and hackathons.

notes.front: Which components do Azure Deployment Environments and Microsoft Dev Box share?
notes.back: Dev centers and projects.
notes.explanation: If you are not configuring Dev Box, you can ignore Dev Box messages you see.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?”, “Components shared with Microsoft Dev Box” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Dev centers and projects are common to both services, and they help organize resources in an enterprise.

notes.front: What can you configure per project and per environment type in Deployment Environments?
notes.back: The target subscription in which the Azure resources are created.
notes.explanation: Project environment types are a subset of the dev center's environment types.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Project environment types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can configure the target subscription in which Azure resources are created per project and per environment type.

notes.front: Which kinds of repository can you attach as a Deployment Environments catalog?
notes.back: A GitHub repository or an Azure DevOps Services repository.
notes.explanation: Microsoft also provides a quick start catalog of sample environment definitions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Catalogs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can attach either a GitHub repository or an Azure DevOps Services repository as a catalog.

notes.front: Which built-in role must developers have on a project to create their own deployment environments?
notes.back: Deployment Environments User.
notes.explanation: DevCenter Project Admin creates environments and manages environment types; Deployment Environments Reader reads others' environments.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Built-in roles” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To enable developers to create their own deployment environments, you must provide access for developers to projects by assigning the Deployment Environments User role.

notes.front: A team's 2,000-line deployment script creates resources step by step and breaks whenever the order changes. What does the Well-Architected guidance suggest?
notes.choices:
A) Add more error handling to the script
B) Move to a declarative tool such as Bicep
C) Deploy by hand in the portal
D) Split the script into ten smaller scripts
notes.back: B) Move to a declarative tool such as Bicep
notes.choicesExplained: A and D keep the imperative approach and its technical debt. C brings back inconsistent manual deployments.
notes.explanation: Declarative files describe only the end state, which is simpler than listing the steps to get there.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Prefer declarative over imperative tools”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Test and production are built from two separate Bicep files that have drifted apart. What should the team do?
notes.choices:
A) Keep both files and compare them monthly
B) Copy the production file over the test file before each release
C) Use one file with parameters for size, count, name and location per environment
D) Build test by hand
notes.back: C) Use one file with parameters for size, count, name and location per environment
notes.choicesExplained: A and B keep two sources of truth. D returns to manual deployment.
notes.explanation: The guidance says to use the same IaC assets everywhere and abstract environment-specific values.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Support multiple environments”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An engineer fixed a production network rule in the portal during an incident, and test no longer matches production. Which policy would have prevented the drift?
notes.back: Deploying all infrastructure changes, configuration included, only through code in pipelines.
notes.explanation: That policy minimises configuration drift and keeps environments consistent.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Linux team already writes YAML and wants one open-source tool to provision Azure virtual machines and then configure the software on them. Which fits?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Machine Configuration in Audit mode
B) A Chef service connection with no Chef server
C) Azure Deployment Environments
D) Ansible with playbooks
notes.back: D) Ansible with playbooks
notes.choicesExplained: A only reports on settings. B needs a Chef automation server to connect to. C gives developers template-based environments, not configuration management.
notes.explanation: Ansible automates provisioning, configuration management and deployment, and its playbooks are written in YAML.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Using Ansible with Azure”, “Using Ansible with Azure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-dev-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Using Ansible you can provision virtual machines, containers, and network and complete cloud infrastructures.

notes.front: A team plans to bring new Linux servers under Azure Automation DSC. What should you advise?
notes.choices:
A) Use Azure Machine Configuration: Automation DSC for Linux retired on 30 September 2023
B) Go ahead; Linux is fully supported
C) Run a self-managed pull server on Windows
D) Use a Chef service connection
notes.back: A) Use Azure Machine Configuration: Automation DSC for Linux retired on 30 September 2023
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the retirement. C does not bring back Linux support. D connects pipelines to Chef, not DSC.
notes.explanation: Automation DSC for Linux has retired, and Machine Configuration is Azure Policy's feature for auditing and configuring settings.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Automation DSC for Linux retirement announcement” (include file) (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Automation DSC for Linux has retired on 30 September 2023.

notes.front: An organisation has 3,000 Windows servers in Azure and on premises and wants central PowerShell DSC configurations with compliance reports. What should it use?
notes.back: Azure Automation State Configuration for now; it retires on 30 September 2027, so plan a move to Azure Machine Configuration.
notes.explanation: It scales across thousands of machines from one central location with compliance reports, but Microsoft asks users to move to Machine Configuration before it retires.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview”, “Why use Azure Automation State Configuration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This service enables scalability across thousands of machines quickly and easily from a central, secure location.

notes.front: An operations team runs its own Windows DSC pull server and is tired of patching it. What can replace it?
notes.choices:
A) A catalog in Deployment Environments
B) An Ansible playbook
C) The built-in pull server in Azure Automation State Configuration
D) The what-if operation
notes.back: C) The built-in pull server in Azure Automation State Configuration
notes.choicesExplained: B configures machines but is not a DSC pull server. A holds IaC templates for environments. D previews template changes.
notes.explanation: The built-in pull server removes the need to run your own, though State Configuration retires on 30 September 2027 in favour of Machine Configuration.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Automation State Configuration overview”, “Built-in pull server” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The built-in pull server in Azure Automation eliminates the need to set up and maintain your own pull server.

notes.front: A security team wants servers to keep a required setting, and any manual change to be reverted automatically. Which Machine Configuration mode fits?
notes.choices:
A) Audit
B) Apply and Monitor
C) Apply and Autocorrect
D) Report-only endpoint
notes.back: C) Apply and Autocorrect
notes.choicesExplained: A only reports. B applies once and monitors but does not correct drift. D is a State Configuration option, not a Machine Configuration mode.
notes.explanation: Apply and Autocorrect brings the machine back into conformance when drift occurs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “Enforcement Modes for Custom Policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Apply and Autocorrect | Configuration applied to the machine and brought back into conformance if drift occurs

notes.front: Compliance wants to know which Azure and on-premises Arc-enabled servers lack a required operating system setting, at scale, without changing them yet. What fits?
notes.back: Azure Machine Configuration assigned through Azure Policy, in Audit mode.
notes.explanation: Machine Configuration audits settings on Azure and Arc-enabled machines and can be orchestrated at scale by Azure Policy.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use the feature directly per-machine, or orchestrate it at scale by using Azure Policy.

notes.front: A template defines a virtual network, a subnet that needs it, and two storage accounts that are independent. How does Resource Manager deploy them?
notes.back: The network before the subnet, in order, and the independent storage accounts in parallel.
notes.explanation: Resource Manager orders interdependent resources and runs others in parallel where possible.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Templates overview”, “Why choose ARM templates?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Resource Manager orchestrates the deployment of interdependent resources so they're created in the correct order.

notes.front: A team finds its JSON templates hard to read and dislikes managing Terraform state files. Which Azure-native option addresses both?
notes.choices:
A) Bicep
B) Larger JSON templates with more comments
C) Ansible dynamic inventory
D) Imperative Azure CLI scripts
notes.back: A) Bicep
notes.choicesExplained: D is imperative and harder to maintain. B keeps the readability problem. C gathers inventory for Ansible, not templates.
notes.explanation: Bicep is more concise than JSON and has no state files to manage because Azure stores state.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Bicep?”, “Benefits of Bicep” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **No state or state files to manage**: Azure stores all states. You can collaborate with others and be confident that your updates are handled as expected.

notes.front: Reviewers want a pipeline to show exactly which resources a Bicep change will create, modify or delete before the deploy stage runs, and to fail if anything is deleted. What should the pipeline run first?
notes.choices:
A) `az deployment group create` in complete mode
B) `az deployment group what-if --no-pretty-print`, then check the JSON
C) `arm-ttk` only
D) An Ansible playbook
notes.back: B) `az deployment group what-if --no-pretty-print`, then check the JSON
notes.choicesExplained: A deploys, and complete mode can delete resources. C tests guidelines but does not predict changes. D configures machines.
notes.explanation: What-if predicts changes without making them, and the JSON output can be inspected by a script.
notes.source: Microsoft, “ARM template deployment what-if operation”, “Azure CLI” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To get a JSON object that you can programmatically inspect for changes, use the `--no-pretty-print` switch.

notes.front: A team keeps ARM templates in Azure Repos and wants every merge to main to deploy them. What should the pipeline use?
notes.back: A pipeline triggered on main that runs the Resource Manager template task.
notes.explanation: The template task lets Azure Pipelines continuously build and deploy ARM template projects.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Templates overview”, “Why choose ARM templates?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By using Azure DevOps and Resource Manager template task, you can use Azure Pipelines to continuously build and deploy ARM template projects.

notes.front: Developers wait days for the platform team to build test infrastructure. The platform team wants self-service but with approved templates and governance. What fits?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Deployment Environments with curated environment definitions
B) Give every developer Owner on the subscription
C) A shared wiki of portal steps
D) Azure Automation State Configuration
notes.back: A) Azure Deployment Environments with curated environment definitions
notes.choicesExplained: B gives up governance. C is manual and inconsistent. D manages machine configuration, not self-service environments.
notes.explanation: Deployment Environments gives developers on-demand infrastructure from approved templates under platform control, but it retires on 22 February 2027, so plan a successor.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?”, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Platform engineers can create and manage environment definitions. To specify which environment definitions are available to developers, platform engineers can associate environment definitions with projects, and assign permissions to developers.

notes.front: A company runs a two-day hackathon; each of 40 attendees needs an identical, isolated environment that is removed afterwards. Which Deployment Environments scenario is this?
notes.choices:
A) Environments as part of a continuous integration and delivery pipeline
B) Sandbox environments for investigations
C) Training, hands-on labs and hackathons
D) On-demand test environments
notes.back: C) Training, hands-on labs and hackathons
notes.choicesExplained: A links lifecycle environments to pipelines. B is for developers exploring technologies. D mimics formal test environments before check-in.
notes.explanation: A project acts as a container for transient activities and can be deleted with all its resources afterwards.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Deployment Environments?”, “Usage scenarios” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can easily delete a project and all related resources when the training is over.

notes.front: Five product teams need the same approved templates and environment types. Where should the platform engineers configure these once?
notes.back: In a dev center that all five teams' projects are associated with.
notes.explanation: A dev center groups projects with similar settings, and its settings apply to each associated project.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Dev centers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you associate a project with a dev center, all the settings for the dev center are automatically applied to the project.

notes.front: A team's sandbox environments must deploy into a low-cost subscription and production into a locked-down one. What do you configure?
notes.choices:
A) Two catalogs
B) Two dev centers
C) Project environment types with a different target subscription each
D) Two environment definitions
notes.back: C) Project environment types with a different target subscription each
notes.choicesExplained: A holds templates, not subscriptions. B would split settings that should be shared. D describe what is deployed, not where.
notes.explanation: The target subscription is configured per project and per environment type.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Project environment types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can configure the target subscription in which Azure resources are created per project and per environment type.

notes.front: One team needs extra templates that other teams must not see. Where should the platform engineer attach the catalog holding them?
notes.back: To that team's project, not to the dev center.
notes.explanation: A catalog attached to a project provides its environment definitions to that project only.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Catalogs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can also attach a catalog to a project to provide environment definitions to that specific project.

notes.front: A platform engineer adds a Bicep file for a web app, database and storage account to the catalog repository, but developers cannot see it. What is most likely missing?
notes.back: The environment file that acts as the manifest; an environment definition needs both the template and that file.
notes.explanation: The template defines the environment and the environment file gives metadata about it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Key concepts for Azure Deployment Environments”, “Environment definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The template defines the environment, and the environment file provides metadata about the template.

notes.front: Declarative versus imperative IaC tools: what does each kind of file describe?
notes.back: Declarative: the desired end state, leaving the system to work out how. Imperative: the steps to run to reach it.
notes.explanation: The guidance prefers declarative tools because their files are simpler.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Mutable versus immutable infrastructure: what happens on each deployment?
notes.back: Mutable: configuration is changed in place. Immutable: it is replaced by new infrastructure running the new configuration.
notes.explanation: Immutable infrastructure must not be changed in place.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”, “Architecture strategies for using infrastructure as code”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Azure Automation State Configuration versus Azure Machine Configuration: what drives each?
notes.back: State Configuration: DSC configurations served by an Automation pull server. Machine Configuration: an Azure Policy feature assigning configurations to machines.
notes.explanation: Machine Configuration can be orchestrated at scale by Azure Policy, including on Arc-enabled machines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?”, “What is Azure Machine Configuration?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Machine configuration uses Azure Policy to dynamically assign configurations to machines.
